result.question: Best practices, current trends, and tooling (mid-2026) for maximizing coding-agent effectiveness and minimizing time-to-mergeable-PR in a large TypeScript monorepo (bun + turborepo, 92 packages, Effect-TS) operated by Claude Code and OpenAI Codex agents. Four dimensions: (1) instruction-file architecture — CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md single-sourcing and generation, per-package nested instruction files, recommended token budgets, machine-enforced rules vs prose; (2) agent context-window economy — skill/progressive-disclosure design patterns, context-optimization tooling such as headroom (github.com/headroomlabs-ai/headroom) and comparable OSS, measured context-cost reduction techniques; (3) agent onboarding & discoverability — symbol indexes, repo navigation aids, conventions that reduce agent churn; (4) CI/local pipeline cycle-time reduction for agent-driven development — local/CI proof parity strategies, turbo remote-cache policies for PR events (read-only cache security tradeoffs), CI runner sizing economics (Blacksmith per-minute billing), PR review-bot consolidation evidence. Prioritize concrete adoptable practices with evidence over generic advice; flag anything that contradicts current practice in repos like ours.
result.summary: For mid-2026 agent-driven development in a large TS monorepo, the highest-leverage, evidence-backed practices are: (1) keep always-loaded instruction files lean and strictly imperative — controlled evaluations show agents reliably follow explicit instructions but repo-overview prose adds >20% inference cost with no general success gain — and layer per-package CLAUDE.md files, which Claude Code loads lazily only when it touches that directory; (2) push all other knowledge behind progressive disclosure (skills with <500-line bodies, one-level-deep references, executable scripts instead of inlined logic), because model recall measurably degrades as context grows ("context rot"); (3) machine-enforce rules that must hold across long sessions via hooks, linters, and CI checks — the largest measured compliance effect is within-session decay (~5.6% lower odds per generated function, median first omission at the 4th function), while file size (25–500 lines) and single-vs-nested file architecture showed no detectable compliance effect; (4) for cycle time, use Turborepo remote caching with a read-only cache policy for PR/untrusted builds (`--remote-cache-read-only`, shipped 2023) and per-minute-billed fast runners like Blacksmith ($0.004/min Ubuntu x64), where the claimed 2x speed multiplier — not the rate cut — drives both cost savings and wall-clock reduction. Two findings contradict folk practice: instruction-file compactness and nested-file splitting are not supported as compliance levers (only as cost levers), and context files per se are a weak lever — enforcement plus context economy are the strong ones.

findings.claim: Layered instruction-file architecture is natively supported and cheap: Claude Code loads the working directory's CLAUDE.md plus all ancestors at launch, and loads per-subdirectory CLAUDE.md files lazily only when it reads files there — so a root file with repo-wide rules plus per-package files costs zero context for packages a task never touches. Directly adoptable in a 92-package monorepo: put slice-specific conventions (e.g. Effect service patterns, schema-first rules per slice) in per-package files rather than the root.
findings.evidence: Verified verbatim against Anthropic's large-codebases doc, including a worked example (starting from packages/api/ loads root + api files with nothing from packages/web/). Caveat: two GitHub issues (#2571, #24987) report on-demand loading failing in specific clients (VS Code extension/WSL2); verify lazy injection fires in your harness before relying on per-package files for correctness-critical rules — though even under that bug, untouched packages still cost nothing.

findings.claim: Repository context files (AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md) are a weak aggregate lever: in controlled evaluations (SWE-bench with LLM-generated files; 138-task AGENTBENCH with developer-committed files; multiple LLMs and agents including Claude Code and Codex), context files did not generally improve task success while raising inference cost >20% on average. The split that matters: explicit instructions ARE reliably followed (tools mentioned in context files used 1.6–2.5x more), but repository-overview sections — popular and provider-recommended — do not help. Actionable: single-source CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md content as terse, non-inferable imperative rules; delete architecture-overview prose (agents rediscover it anyway); developer-written files beat LLM-generated ones only marginally (~4pp). This contradicts common practice of front-loading repo tours into instruction files, including overview-style content in repos like ours.
findings.evidence: Three unanimous 3-0 claims from one primary academic source (ETH Zurich SRI Lab + LogicStar.ai, revised 2026-06-23), corroborated by InfoQ/Engineer's Codex coverage; abstract quotes verified verbatim. Qualifiers: Python-only repos, single-issue SWE-bench-style tasks; context files DID help (+2.7%) when repo documentation was stripped, and remain useful for non-standard/non-inferable practices — which is exactly what a bun+turbo+Effect-TS monorepo has in abundance, so the takeaway is 'instructions yes, overviews no', not 'delete the file'.

findings.claim: Instruction-file size and file-splitting architecture are not compliance levers: across 1,650 controlled Claude Code sessions, CLAUDE.md length (25–500 lines) produced no detectable compliance effect with affirmative Bayesian null support (BF10=0.096), and single CLAUDE.md vs +AGENTS.md vs +two nested per-directory files showed no detectable difference (ICR 67.7%/68.2%/61.7%, p=0.19; effects >~6pp ruled out; the nested condition actually trended worst). Splitting instructions into per-package files is not supported as a compliance remediation — do it for context-cost reasons (lazy loading), not adherence reasons.
findings.evidence: Two unanimous 3-0 claims, all figures verified against the full PDF (McMillan, HxAI Australia, May 2026). Downgraded from high because it is a single-author non-peer-reviewed preprint, compliance was operationalized as one trivial syntactic marker (// @tracked), tested on two TypeScript codebases with Claude Code only — transfer to demanding multi-rule instruction sets and Codex is untested. The architecture null is failure-to-reject (no Bayes support), unlike the size null. Note the paper explicitly frames the size finding as 'in tension with practitioner advice' to keep files compact — the compactness rationale that survives is token cost (see context-rot finding), not adherence.

findings.claim: The dominant compliance failure mode is within-session decay, and the remedy is machine enforcement, not prose: each additional function generated in a session correlated with ~5.6% lower odds of following a CLAUDE.md instruction (OR=0.944, p≈1e-49), median first omission at the 4th generated function — the largest effect the factorial study measured. Author's recommendation, aligned with the file-architecture nulls: for rules that must hold across long sessions, use agent hooks that re-surface rules mid-session (PreToolUse/PostToolUse/Stop), linters, and CI checks rather than tuning instruction-file structure. Maps directly onto machine-enforced-rules-over-prose: lint policies, tsgo diagnostics, and yeet-style gates are the reliable channel; CLAUDE.md prose is the unreliable one.
findings.evidence: 3-0 vote; all statistics verified against the primary PDF including the non-monotonicity qualifier. Caveats: the decay finding was identified post-hoc and the paper itself says it 'warrants independent replication'; detectable on only 2 of 3 multi-function tasks (per-task ORs 1.005/0.955/0.831), so the pooled figure averages heterogeneity; single preprint, Claude Code only.

findings.claim: Context is a finite attention budget with measurable decay ('context rot'): model recall accuracy degrades as context-window token count grows, which is Anthropic's stated rationale for lean always-loaded files and just-in-time context loading — agents should hold lightweight identifiers (file paths, queries, links) and pull data into context at runtime via tools rather than pre-loading corpora. Hybrid strategies (some up-front retrieval for speed) are acknowledged as optimal in practice.
findings.evidence: Two unanimous 3-0 claims; quotes verified verbatim against the Anthropic engineering post (2025-09-29), with independent empirical corroboration (Chroma's 18-model study: all models degrade with input length; lost-in-the-middle literature). Anthropic reinforced the position through the Agent Skills architecture, current mid-2026. Fair qualifier: degradation magnitude varies by model/task — simple lexical needle recall stays near-perfect; degradation is clearest on semantic/reasoning tasks, which is what coding agents do.

findings.claim: Skill design has concrete, documented token-budget rules implementing three-tier progressive disclosure: (a) only name+description frontmatter is pre-loaded at startup; SKILL.md body is read on trigger; bundled files on demand — per-skill standing cost is frontmatter only; (b) keep SKILL.md under 500 lines, splitting overflow into referenced files; (c) keep references one level deep from SKILL.md (Claude may head -100 nested references and get incomplete information) and give files >100 lines a table of contents to survive partial reads; (d) ship deterministic logic as executable scripts (bash-executed, only output costs tokens) instead of prose; (e) keep skill descriptions short and keyword-led — with many skills (repo-root sessions can accumulate 'into the hundreds'), descriptions get truncated to a ~1%-of-context budget, least-used first, which can strip the trigger keywords used for selection.
findings.evidence: Five unanimous 3-0 claims across multiple primary Anthropic doc pages, all quotes verified verbatim on live pages (2026-07-05), corroborated by third-party teardowns and directly observable in Claude Code sessions. Caveats: Claude-specific vendor guidance (behavioral heuristics, not benchmarks); transfer to Codex agents not established by these sources; truncation is also mitigable via settings (skillListingBudgetFraction, skillOverrides 'name-only') — short descriptions are best practice, not the only remedy.

findings.claim: Headroom (github.com/headroomlabs-ai/headroom; ~57k stars, v0.30.0 released 2026-07-03) is the leading OSS context-compression layer: vendor-published claim of 60–95% fewer input tokens on tool outputs, logs, files, RAG chunks, and conversation history 'same answers', with concrete per-workload numbers — code search 17,765→1,408 tokens (92%), SRE incident debugging 65,694→5,118 (92%), GitHub issue triage 54,174→14,761 (73%), codebase exploration 78,502→41,254 (47%) — plus self-run accuracy-preservation evals (GSM8K/TruthfulQA/SQuAD v2/BFCL, deltas ±0.000 to +0.030) and a published reproduction command. Deployable as library, proxy, or MCP server.
findings.evidence: Two unanimous 3-0 claims verified verbatim against the repo README/description. Confidence capped at medium for real-world applicability: all figures are vendor self-reported benchmark ceilings, not independent replications; third-party review notes gains are heavily content-type-dependent (top-of-range rows are structured JSON/code/logs via SmartCrusher/CodeCompressor; plain-prose gains much smaller). Treat as 'Headroom's published numbers', pilot-measure on your own tool-output mix before counting savings.

findings.claim: A measured design point for compaction tooling: on a 50-task long-horizon GPT-5 tool-use benchmark, adding automated summarization of evicted history (summary window 3) on top of recency pruning raised complete task success from 79.0% to 91.6% at only 3.4% token overhead over pruning alone — i.e., cheap summarization of what you evict recovers most of the accuracy risk of aggressive pruning. Importantly, the companion claim that pruning ALONE improved accuracy was refuted in verification — do not take 'aggressive truncation is free' as the lesson; the survivor is 'prune + summarize evictions'.
findings.evidence: 3-0 vote; all numbers verified against the primary preprint (Lodha et al., Microsoft, June 2026; 5-run averages with CIs). Major caveat: the benchmark is enterprise expense-itemization via MCP in Dynamics 365 — not coding — so this is a design-point datum for compaction architecture, not a transferable coding-agent number. ~1-month-old unreviewed preprint, no replications yet.

findings.claim: For agent onboarding/discoverability, language-server-backed symbol navigation is the recommended replacement for grep/file-scan discovery: official Anthropic LSP plugins exist for TypeScript and 10 other languages (`/plugin install typescript-lsp@claude-plugins-official`), letting agents jump to definitions, find references, and surface type errors instead of scanning the tree — at the cost of requiring the language-server binary (typescript-language-server) on each machine. Caveats from the docs themselves: availability varies by language/environment, language servers can consume significant memory on large projects, and monorepo workspaces may emit false-positive unresolved-import diagnostics. Complements (does not replace) repo-level conventions like symbol-discovery skills and export catalogs already in use here.
findings.evidence: 3-0 vote; install command, marketplace name, 11-language plugin table, and binary requirement all verified verbatim across two official doc pages plus the GitHub repo; corroborated by third-party writeups (CircleCI, Scott Spence) and by the built-in LSP tool observable in Claude Code environments.

findings.claim: Turborepo remote-cache policy for agent-heavy CI: the core cycle-time value is sharing one cache across all machines and CI so identical tasks never re-execute (independently measured at ~50% turbo task-duration / ~30% total CI job reduction by Mercari); and the security-correct PR policy is privilege separation — trusted main-branch CI gets read/write while PR/untrusted builds get read-only via the native `--remote-cache-read-only` flag (shipped in vercel/turbo#6624, merged 2023-11-28, closing issue #1188 whose explicit motivation was preventing less-trusted environments from poisoning shared cache artifacts; flag confirmed present in turbo 2.10.3). Critical negative result: the companion claim that HMAC-SHA256 artifact signing (signature:true + TURBO_REMOTE_CACHE_SIGNATURE_KEY) is the documented cache-poisoning mitigation was REFUTED 0-3 in verification — treat read-only token separation, not artifact signing, as the verified control for PR events.
findings.evidence: Three unanimous 3-0 claims verified against live vendor docs and GitHub primary data (issue/PR timestamps, verbatim issue body, flag present in local turbo 2.10.3 --help). Qualifiers: cache gains depend on artifact size vs network round-trip; the flag's official docs describe it neutrally — the security framing comes from the originating issue and ecosystem practice (ducktors/turborepo-remote-cache #199 requests the same for the same reason).

findings.claim: CI runner economics for agent-driven PR volume: Blacksmith bills Ubuntu x64 runners at $0.004/min (2 vCPU base; larger sizes bill proportionally; 3,000 free min/mo), framing 'up to 67% total cost savings' vs GitHub-hosted — decomposed by the vendor as 2x faster runtime plus 33% cheaper per-minute. The analytical point for time-to-mergeable-PR: the speed multiplier, not the rate, drives ~75% of the advertised savings and ALL of the cycle-time reduction — so runner selection should be evaluated on measured wall-clock speedup for your workload, with the per-minute rate as a secondary tiebreaker.
findings.evidence: Two unanimous 3-0 claims; pricing and framing verified verbatim on the live pricing page (2026-07-05) and repeated by independent 2026 comparisons (BetterStack, jmduke) without dispute; RunsOn benchmarks place Blacksmith among top single-thread x64 managed runners. Medium because the 2x/67% figures are vendor marketing, not independent measurement — real speedups vary by workload (vendor case studies claim 2.3x–5.9x); the $0.004/min rate itself is high-confidence.

result.caveats: Source-quality gradients matter here: (1) Headroom's 60–95% and Blacksmith's 2x/67% figures are vendor self-reported — accurately attributed but not independently replicated; pilot-measure before budgeting on them. (2) The two most decision-relevant academic results are single non-peer-reviewed preprints with domain gaps: the file-size/architecture/decay factorial study (2605.10039) used one trivial syntactic compliance marker on Claude Code only, and the 91.6%-with-summarization result (2606.10209) is from enterprise expense workflows, not coding; the AGENTS.md evaluation (2602.11988) is Python single-issue tasks, so its null may understate context-file value in a convention-heavy Effect-TS monorepo where non-inferable instructions dominate. (3) Skill/CLAUDE.md loading mechanics are Claude-specific; transfer to Codex agents is asserted nowhere in the verified sources, so a single-sourced AGENTS.md generation pipeline must be validated per-harness. (4) Two refuted claims change recommendations: turbo HMAC artifact signing did NOT survive verification as the documented cache-poisoning mitigation (use read-only token separation), and 'pruning alone improves accuracy' did not survive (pruning needs summarization on top). (5) Coverage gaps: no claims survived on PR review-bot consolidation evidence or on local/CI proof-parity strategies, both explicitly asked in the research question — those dimensions are unanswered, not settled. (6) Time-sensitivity: vendor docs, plugin marketplaces, and runner pricing (including GitHub's March 2026 platform-fee change) are moving targets; lazy per-directory CLAUDE.md loading has open client-specific bug reports (VS Code/WSL2).
openQuestions: Does the within-session compliance-decay effect (and the corresponding hooks/linters-over-prose remedy) replicate for substantive multi-rule instruction sets and for OpenAI Codex harnesses, not just a trivial marker under Claude Code?

What is empirically the best mitigation stack for Turborepo remote-cache poisoning on PR events given the HMAC-signing claim failed verification — is signature verification currently real and sufficient, or is read-only token separation plus artifact provenance the only defensible policy?

Is there any independent, coding-domain measurement of context-compression middleware (Headroom or comparable) on agent task-success and time-to-mergeable-PR, as opposed to vendor token-reduction benchmarks?

What evidence exists for PR review-bot consolidation (fewer, better-integrated reviewers vs many overlapping bots) and for local/CI proof-parity strategies — the two sub-questions on which zero claims survived verification?

refuted.claim: Pruning agent context to only the last 5 tool call/response pairs reduced token consumption by 63.9% (535,274 vs 1,480,996 tokens) while simultaneously improving task completion from 71.0% to 79.0% on a 50-task GPT-5 enterprise tool-use benchmark — i.e., aggressive context truncation improved, not degraded, long-horizon agent accuracy.

Turborepo supports cryptographic artifact integrity via HMAC-SHA256 signing, enabled with `signature: true` in turbo.json's remoteCache options plus a TURBO_REMOTE_CACHE_SIGNATURE_KEY environment variable; artifacts failing verification are treated as cache misses rather than errors. This is the documented mitigation for cache-poisoning risk when untrusted contexts (e.g., PR events) can write to a shared cache.
